passage:
MOTHO KE MOTHO KA BATHO BABANG – Jeremy Cronin
(A Person is a Person Because of Other People)

By holding my mirror out of the window I see 
Clear to the end of the passage.
There's a person down there.
A prisoner polishing a doorhandle.
In the mirror I see him see 
My face in the mirror,
I see the fingertips of his free hand
Bunch together, as if to make
An object the size of a badge
Which travels up to his forehead 
The place of an imaginary cap. (This means: A warder.)
Two fingers are extended in a vee
And wiggle like two antennae. (He's being watched.) 
A finger of his free hand makes a watch-hand's arc
On the wrist of his polishing arm without
Disrupting the slow-slow rhythm of his work. (Later. Maybe later we can speak.)
Hey! Wat maak jy daar? 
– a voice from around the corner.
No. Just polishing baas.
He turns back to me, now watch
His free hand, the talkative one,
Slips silently behind
– Strength brother, it says,
In my mirror,
A black fist.
question: The poem illustrates how political prisoners provide support to one another in intolerable circumstances. By close reference to diction, tone and structure, discuss how the above statement is reflected in the poem. Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 250–300 words.
memo: Candidates should cover the following points (among others) with reference to the rubric: $\checkmark$ The speaker and prisoner use the mirror as an ingenious means of communication in solitary confinement $\checkmark$ Use of signals (antennae, watch-hand arc) to offer support/camaraderie/sanity $\checkmark$ Repetition of 'I see' emphasises comfort in acknowledging presence $\checkmark$ Ironic use of 'free hand' and 'talkative' shows humour amidst hardship $\checkmark$ '(Later. Maybe later we can speak)' provides hope $\checkmark$ 'Strength brother' and the 'black fist' convey solidarity/defiance $\checkmark$ Tone of the warder 'Hey! Wat maak jy daar?' is threatening/harsh, contrasting with prisoner solidarity $\checkmark$ Prisoner's reply 'No, just polishing baas' is submissive to avoid punishment $\checkmark$ Structure: narrative on left, translations in brackets highlight the need for secrecy and value of contact $\checkmark$ Enjambment suggests natural flow and intimacy despite separation.
final_answer: Essay response assessing the theme of support among political prisoners through literary devices.

question: Refer to lines 13–16: 'The stars are … to any good.' Comment on how the diction in these lines conveys the speaker's mood.

passage:
Felix Randal the farrier, O he is dead then? my duty all ended, 
Who have watched his mould of man, big-boned and hardy-handsome
Pining, pining, till time when reason rambled in it and some
Fatal four disorders, fleshed there, all contended? 

Sickness broke him. Impatient he cursed at first, but mended
Being anointed and all; though a heavenlier heart began some
Months earlier, since I had our sweet reprieve and ransom
Tendered to him. Ah well, God rest him all road ever he offended! 

This seeing the sick endears them to us, us too it endears.
My tongue had taught thee comfort, touch had quenched thy tears,
Thy tears that touched my heart, child, Felix, poor Felix Randal;

How far from then forethought of, all thy more boisterous years,
When thou at the random grim forge, powerful amidst peers,
Didst fettle for the great grey drayhorse his bright and battering sandal!
question: What is the speaker's intention when he describes Felix Randal as 'mould of man' (line 2)?
memo: Felix Randal is described as the epitome of manliness. $\checkmark$ The speaker's intention is to highlight Felix's commendable qualities. $\checkmark$ /He creates a favourable impression of Felix's attributes and strength which other men might emulate. $\checkmark$
final_answer: The speaker intends to highlight Felix Randal's epitome of manliness and commendable qualities, creating a favourable impression of his strength and attributes.

passage:
BURNING THE FIRE BREAK – Ingrid Andersen

I'm called from my books,
this peaceful space
away from you.

The wind has whipped
the fire out
of control, it threatens the farmhouse:
all hands are needed.

I stand, armed with beater,
upon the border of veld and garden.
I think of National Geographic,
of fires in Australia, California –
I've not done this before.

Smoke burns bitter in my throat.
There. In the haze,
flames at the base 
of the khakibos
in the close-grazed stubble
five strides ahead of me.

The wind behind them 
suddenly shoves.

The fire flings up, 
reaches into 
longer grass nearby:
an angry wall that
spits and roars
towards me.

I face the flame,
stand firm.

You shall not pass.
question: Refer to lines 8–9: 'I stand, armed … veld and garden.' What does the word, 'armed' suggest about the speaker's view of the fire?

final_answer: The speaker views the fire as an enemy or intruder that must be defended against.

topic: The Picture of Dorian Gray – Essay Question
passage: Dorian Gray must take responsibility for his own fate. Critically discuss the extent to which you agree with the above statement. Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 400–450 words ($2	ext{–}2 rac{1}{2}$ pages).
question: Dorian Gray must take responsibility for his own fate. Critically discuss the extent to which you agree with the above statement.
memo: Candidates might argue that Dorian is entirely responsible for his fate, or they might argue that he is only partly responsible as there are other contributing factors. $\checkmark$ Arguments for Dorian's responsibility include: his inherent selfishness and self-absorption, his conscious choice to adopt Lord Henry's theories of Hedonism and Aestheticism, his initial wish for the portrait to age instead of him, his influence by the 'yellow book', his cruel treatment of Sybil Vane, his lack of willpower to change despite self-disgust, his refusal to accept accountability when confronted by Basil, and his murder of Basil. $\checkmark$ Arguments for external responsibility include: Basil's portrait fueling his narcissism, Basil introducing him to the corruptive influence of Lord Henry, and Lord Henry consciously using Dorian as a 'scientific experiment' to corrupt an impressionable youth. $\checkmark$ [Credit valid alternative/mixed responses. Refer to the standard rubric for essay assessment.]
final_answer: Candidates must write an essay evaluating Dorian Gray's agency versus external influences (Lord Henry/Basil) in his moral downfall.

subject: english_hl
question: Suggest why Lord Henry has drawn Dorian's attention to the inquest into Sibyl's death.
memo: Lord Henry had previously cautioned Dorian from getting involved in the inquest as it might be damaging to his reputation. $\checkmark$ He probably thinks that Dorian might be interested in knowing the outcome and will feel relieved/reassured to know that he has not been connected to Sibyl's death. $\checkmark$ In Lord Henry's mind, this should bring closure to any feelings of love and/or guilt Dorian might still be feeling for Sibyl. $\checkmark$
final_answer: Lord Henry wants to reassure Dorian that he is not linked to the death, provide closure to Dorian's guilt, and manage the situation before it damages Dorian's reputation.

subject: english_hl
question: Refer to lines 13–14: 'He frowned, and … the pieces away' and line 16: 'Victor might have read it.' Account for Dorian's response in these lines.
memo: Dorian is irritated as he does not want to be reminded of the unsavoury circumstances of Sibyl's death. $\checkmark$ Tearing the report is his way of denying the unpleasantness and removing evidence of his connection. $\checkmark$ He is afraid his servant might realise the link and discover the changes occurring on his portrait; his paranoia is evident. $\checkmark$
final_answer: Dorian reacts with irritation and denial to remove evidence of his connection to the death, driven by paranoia that his servants might uncover his secrets.

subject: english_hl
question: Lord Henry's note makes reference to 'a book that might interest [Dorian Gray]' (lines 2–3). Using your knowledge of the novel as a whole, comment on the role this book plays in Dorian's life.
memo: The yellow book acts as a guiding force in Dorian's life, as he is enraptured by the hedonistic lifestyle of the protagonist. $\checkmark$ He attempts to emulate this lifestyle, which encourages him to blur the lines between virtue and vice. $\checkmark$ He eventually recognises it as a 'poisonous book' that caused him harm. $\checkmark$
final_answer: The book serves as a catalyst for Dorian's hedonism, encouraging him to abandon moral constraints, though he later acknowledges it as a corrupting 'poisonous' influence.

subject: english_hl
question: Refer to line 14: 'How ugly it … ugliness made things!' Discuss how Dorian's avoidance of ugliness ultimately leads to his destruction.
memo: Dorian is encouraged by aesthetic principles to seek beauty and avoid the unpleasant reality, leading to his wish that the portrait ages instead of him. $\checkmark$ This grants him immunity from accountability, enabling his depraved acts and causing his soul (represented by the portrait) to become tarnished. $\checkmark$ His inability to confront the ugliness of his soul in the portrait eventually drives him to destroy the portrait and himself. $\checkmark$
final_answer: By prioritising aesthetic beauty over morality, Dorian seeks to escape accountability; this ultimately manifests in the corrupt portrait, which he destroys along with his own life.

subject: english_hl
question: Place the above extract in context.

question: Refer to line 14: 'The drowsy sailor … looked wildly around.' Comment on the sailor's reaction in this line.
memo: The sailor is James Vane; hearing the name 'Prince Charming' causes him to jump up because he has spent years tracking down the man who destroyed his sister Sibyl. $\checkmark$ He swore to kill the man responsible for harming her. $\checkmark$ He now realises he has the opportunity to discover the identity of 'Prince Charming' and exact his revenge. $\checkmark$
final_answer: James Vane reacts with sudden intensity because he recognises the name 'Prince Charming', which identifies the man who caused his sister's death and whom he has sworn to kill.

subject: english_hl
question: Refer to line 23: 'In her dealings with man Destiny never closed her accounts.' Comment on the effectiveness of this image in the context of the novel.
memo: Destiny is personified as an accountant collecting debts, which is effective because Dorian believes the portrait grants him permanent immunity. $\checkmark$ It highlights the inevitability of consequences for his sinful actions. $\checkmark$ Although he tries to escape, the image conveys that one cannot ultimately avoid paying for one's sins. $\checkmark$
final_answer: The image effectively personifies Destiny as an unyielding accountant, emphasising that regardless of Dorian's belief in his immunity, he will ultimately be held accountable for his transgressions.

subject: english_hl
question: Dorian is referred to as both 'the devil's bargain' (line 10) and 'Prince Charming' (line 12). Critically discuss what these names suggest about the contradictory nature of Dorian's character.
memo: The names illustrate the duality of Dorian as both refined, sophisticated, and outwardly beautiful ('Prince Charming') and corrupt, sinful, and manipulative ('the devil's bargain'). $\checkmark$ His public appearance masks his degenerate lifestyle. $\checkmark$ The portrait allows him to maintain his 'Prince Charming' façade while he engages in immoral acts like the murder of Basil and the ruin of others. $\checkmark$ The coexistence of these labels highlights his hypocrisy and the depth of his moral decay beneath his pristine exterior. $\checkmark$
final_answer: The names contrast Dorian's public, idealized image of 'Prince Charming' with the reality of his corrupted soul and immoral actions, encapsulated by the term 'the devil's bargain', highlighting his fundamental hypocrisy.

question: Refer to line 17: 'I watched sullenly as he loudly appreciated my gift'. Explain what this line suggests about Pi's attitude toward Richard Parker at this point in the novel.

question: In light of your knowledge of the novel as a whole, discuss the significance of Richard Parker's presence on the lifeboat.
memo: Pi's second story suggests that Richard Parker is created as Pi's alter-ego. His presence makes the reader aware of the brutality to which Pi resorts to survive his ordeal.
